title: Personal Finance: Final Assessment
description: A final assessment covering the key ideas from all three lessons. Reach the passing score to complete the course.

history.note: AI-written question draft. Not reviewed or approved by a human (admin); do not give to students.

passing.note: Proposed: 7 of 10 questions (70%). Not approved by a teacher (admin); completion is not recognized until approved.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: Chris earns $3,000 a month in gross pay, and deductions take 18% of it. Chris plans to save 20% of net (take-home) income. How many dollars a month will Chris save? (Enter a number only.)
Hypothetical example: Dana wants to free up $50 in next month's budget. Which change can she most likely make the fastest?

choices.text: Move to an apartment with cheaper rent
Change the terms of her yearly phone contract
Spend less on eating out and entertainment
Switch to a car loan with lower payments

questions.prompt: Which of these is the best example of a SMART financial goal?

choices.text: Save $900 for a laptop in 12 months by setting aside $75 a month
Save a lot more money this year than I did last year
Try to spend less on things I do not really need
Become better with money and stop wasting it soon

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: Maya opens a savings account with $1,500. It pays a 4.8% APR, compounded monthly, and she makes no other deposits or withdrawals for one year. How much is in the account at the end of the year? Round to the nearest cent, and round only at the final step. (Enter a number only.)
Hypothetical example: Your savings account pays 2% a year, and prices rise 3% over the same year. What happens to the purchasing power of your savings?

choices.text: It rises by about 2%, because the account balance grows
It stays the same, because interest is paid on the balance
It rises by about 5%, the sum of interest and inflation
It falls by about 1%, because prices rise faster than the balance

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: Loan X and Loan Y are each $5,000 for three years at the same 8% interest rate. Loan Y also charges a $150 fee to set up the loan. If the disclosed APR includes this fee, how do the two loans compare?

choices.text: Both APRs are 8%, because the interest rates are equal
Loan Y has the higher APR, because it costs more in total
Loan X has the higher APR, because Y's fee lowers its rate
Loan Y has the lower APR, because fees are paid up front

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: For ten years, Grace keeps all her savings in cash in a drawer at home, while prices rise every year. Which risk is she most clearly exposed to?

choices.text: Inflation risk
Market risk
Credit risk
Liquidity risk

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A lender wants an expected return of 3% on one-year loans. It expects 5% of borrowers to default and repay nothing. Using (1 + i)(1 − default share) = 1 + target return, what interest rate i must it charge, in percent? Round to two decimal places. (Enter a number only.)
Hypothetical example: A program in Country V helps rural women open mobile money accounts linked to a savings feature and simple insurance. Which SDG target does this most directly support?

choices.text: Target 8.5, equal pay for work of equal value
Target 1.1, eradicating extreme poverty for everyone
Target 8.6, fewer young people out of school or work
Target 1.4, equal access to financial services for all

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A friend says, "Fund Z returned 15% a year for the last three years, so it will keep doing that. Put your emergency fund in it." What is the best response?

choices.text: Agree, because three good years show the fund has a reliable return
Agree, as long as the fund's fees are lower than a savings account's
Disagree: past returns do not guarantee future ones, and emergency money needs stability
Disagree, because funds with high past returns tend to lose money next
